screens.title: Blackboard — Shared Memory for AI
screens.narratorSegment: A Blackboard is simply a structured key-value store used by an AI Controller and its Behavior Tree to share state across nodes. Define keys like TargetActor (object), PatrolLocation (vector), or Alerted (bool) and let any Task, Decorator, or Service read or write them. This centralization prevents tight coupling between nodes: a Move To task doesn’t need direct references to the sensing code because it reads the TargetActor key. Concretely, when AIPerception senses the player, the AI Controller sets TargetActor in the Blackboard. The chase Sequence has a Blackboard-based decorator that queries Is Set for TargetActor; when true, the Sequence runs a Move To task using that key. One common misconception is to treat the Blackboard like a global state bag you can overpopulate; instead keep keys explicit and minimal to avoid confusion and costly lookups. Also remember that sharing a Blackboard asset across multiple AI pawns is uncommon; typically each AI has an instance-bound Blackboard Component. When debugging, open the Behavior Tree Monitor and watch the Blackboard tab — you will see keys change in real time which tells you whether the Behavior Tree has data to proceed. How would you structure keys for an AI that can switch between patrol, investigate, and attack?

keyIdea.title: Blackboard principle
keyIdea.text: Use small, explicit keys to share state across tree nodes and decouple perception, logic, and actions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Blackboard
Definition

Blackboard: Key-Value Store

A Blackboard is a centralized memory where nodes read and write values used to control Behavior Tree flow.

Common Keys
  • TargetActor — Object (Actor)
  • PatrolLocation — Vector
  • Alerted — Bool
Best Practice
Keep keys explicit and limited. Avoid using a single catch-all key for many unrelated values.
Key Takeaway

Blackboards decouple perception from action by providing a shared, named memory for your Behavior Tree.

Concrete Example
Use AIPerception's OnTargetPerceptionUpdated to Set Value As Object on the Blackboard when the player is sensed, and Clear Value when lost. The chase Sequence checks TargetActor Is Set to decide whether to run.
Common Mistake
Treating the Blackboard as global shared memory for every pawn. Usually give each AI its own Blackboard Component instance.
Check your understanding
Which key would you add to support a 'take cover' behavior and how would a Service update it?

screens.title: Behavior Tree Anatomy
screens.narratorSegment: A Behavior Tree is a hierarchical structure that orchestrates AI decisions. At the root sits the Root node, beneath it Composites like Selector and Sequence control execution order. A Selector tries each child until one succeeds, which is ideal for prioritized choices such as Attack, then Chase, then Patrol. A Sequence executes children in order and fails if any child fails; use it when steps must happen in a strict order, for example Find Cover then Shoot. Decorators are conditional gates placed above nodes — they check Blackboard keys or visibility and allow a branch only if conditions pass. Tasks are leaf nodes that perform actions, like Move To or Play Animation. Services are special nodes that run periodically while their branch is active to update Blackboard keys or perform checks. A misconception is to overuse Services for per-frame checks; prefer half-second intervals and only update what changes. In practice you'll combine these: a Sequence decorated with a 'TargetActor Is Set' decorator contains a Service that refreshes target location and a Move To task that reads that location. Understanding how these parts connect helps you design trees that are both reactive and maintainable. What decision should a Selector prioritize in your game design?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Behavior Tree Anatomy
Structure

Composites, Decorators, Tasks, Services

Use selectors for priority, sequences for ordered steps, decorators for gating, tasks to act, and services to keep data fresh.

Selector Example
Try Attack, then Chase, then Patrol. Stops at the first successful branch.
Sequence Example
Find Cover → MoveToCover → Shoot. Sequence fails if Find Cover cannot find a spot.
Key Takeaway

Mix node types intentionally: priority, order, conditions, actions, and periodic updates are distinct responsibilities.

Visual Cards
Decorator
Checks a condition like 'TargetActor Is Set' or 'Has Line of Sight To'.
Service
Runs periodically to update Blackboard keys such as CurrentTargetLocation.
Task
Performs actions: Move To, Play Animation, or custom Blueprint tasks.
Common Misconception
Using Services for constant heavy tracing. Prefer timed updates and event-driven checks where possible to save CPU.

screens.title: Perception → Blackboard → Tree
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the concrete process of turning perception into action. The AIPerception component raises an OnTargetPerceptionUpdated event when it senses or loses an actor. In the AI Controller, respond to that event by getting the Blackboard Component and calling Set Value As Object for TargetActor when the player is sensed, and Clear Value when lost. The Behavior Tree’s Chase branch must have a Blackboard-based decorator configured to query Is Set for TargetActor so it activates only when that key exists. To keep the chase accurate when the target moves, add a Service that runs periodically and writes the target's current location into a CurrentTargetLocation or PatrolLocation key. The Move To task should read that key from the Blackboard, or use the Blackboard Key pointing to the actor directly. One typical mistake is forgetting to Run Behavior Tree on BeginPlay in the AI Controller — the tree never runs even if the Blackboard changes. Another debugging step is to open the Behavior Tree Monitor and confirm that the decorator becomes green and the Move To task receives updated positions. As you practice, think about how often your Service needs to run for acceptable responsiveness without wasting C P U.

keyIdea.title: Event-driven flow
keyIdea.text: Use AIPerception events to set Blackboard keys and Services to refresh dynamic target data for moving actors.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Perception to Action
Process

AIPerception → Blackboard → Behavior Tree

Respond to perception events by updating Blackboard values that drive tree decorators and tasks.

Step-by-step
  1. On perception success: Set Value As Object(TargetActor).
  2. On perception lost: Clear Value(TargetActor).
  3. Behavior Tree decorator checks TargetActor Is Set to run Chase Sequence.
  4. Service updates current actor location periodically for Move To accuracy.
Key Takeaway

Link perception events to Blackboard updates so the tree always has the data needed to act.

Concrete Example
[AIPerceptionComponent OnTargetPerceptionUpdated]
    -> [Branch] (Condition: Successfully Sensed && Is Player Character)
        [True]
            -> [Get Blackboard Component (self)]
            -> [Set Value As Object (TargetActor, Perceived Actor)]
        [False] (Player Lost)
            -> [Get Blackboard Component (self)]
            -> [Clear Value (TargetActor)]
Debug Tip
If the tree doesn't chase, confirm Run Behavior Tree is called on BeginPlay and check the Decorator configuration in the Behavior Tree Monitor.

screens.title: Tasks, Services, Decorators — Practical Blueprints
screens.narratorSegment: Tasks are the leaf actions of a Behavior Tree and should represent a single atomic activity, like moving, attacking, or triggering an animation. Services run periodically while a branch is active to update Blackboard keys or perform cheap checks that inform decorators. Decorators evaluate conditions to allow or block branch execution. Choose a custom Blueprint task when you need game-specific work such as selecting a cover point or playing a complex combo animation sequence. Create a Service when you need to refresh data like the target's moving location; for example, a BTS_UpdateTargetLocation service can run every 0.5 seconds to set CurrentTargetLocation on the Blackboard. A common mistake is to pack too much logic into a Task that should instead be a Service plus small tasks — Tasks should finish with success or failure and not run indefinitely. When authoring a Decorator, prefer simple checks: Blackboard Based Condition or Has Line Of Sight To. Use the Behavior Tree Monitor to observe decorator outcomes and service ticks; this will reveal misconfigured keys or improper query types. Consider how you would split behavior between a custom MoveTo wrapper task and services that compute the destination.

keyIdea.title: Node responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Keep Tasks focused, Services time-sliced, and Decorators simple gates; split complex logic across nodes to remain debuggable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Tasks & Services
Write Small Tasks

Custom Tasks & Services

Design tasks to do one thing and finish. Use services to keep data fresh without blocking execution.

Example Service
BTS_UpdateTargetLocation — runs every 0.5s, reads TargetActor, writes CurrentTargetLocation.
Example Task
BTT_FindRandomPatrolLocation — finds a random navigable point, sets PatrolLocation, finishes success.
Key Takeaway

Favor small, testable nodes. Use services sparingly and measure their cost when many AI run in parallel.

Blueprint Pattern
// BTS_UpdateTargetLocation (pseudo-Blueprint steps)
Event ReceiveTickAI(OwnerController, ControlledPawn)
  -> Get Blackboard Component
  -> Get Value As Object(TargetActor)
  -> If TargetActor != null
      -> Get Actor Location
      -> Set Value As Vector(CurrentTargetLocation, ActorLocation)
Misconception
Placing heavy game logic inside a Task that never finishes. Tasks should return success or fail so the tree can continue making decisions.

screens.title: NavMesh & Nav Areas
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's NavMesh provides the foundation for AI pathfinding and supports dynamic updates when geometry changes. Nav Areas are tags you assign to geometry to influence routing; for instance, a NavArea_Danger can carry a higher traversal cost so AI prefers a longer, safer route. Always verify Agent Radius and Agent Height in Project Settings -> Navigation Mesh so collision shapes match your pawn; mismatches commonly cause characters to get stuck in doorways. For dynamic scenarios like opened doors or collapsing walls, the NavMesh can be rebuilt or updated at runtime so AI recalculates valid paths. When many agents navigate, use Crowd Manager to tune separation and avoidance so movement looks natural. A common trap is setting cell sizes too small: while this yields finer paths, it increases memory and generation time. Conversely, too large a cell size makes the NavMesh blocky. When AI must follow a moving target, make the Move To node read a Blackboard key that a Service refreshes, ensuring the path is recalculated as the target moves. Consider how you might use a NavArea_Jump to mark spots where AI must use a jump path instead of walking.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › NavMesh & Nav Areas
Concept

NavMesh, Areas, and Agent Settings

Nav Areas assign traversal cost and behavior to geometry; agent settings control what the agent can fit through.

Nav Areas Example
Assign NavArea_Danger to hazardous regions and increase cost so AI avoids them when possible.
Agent Settings
Set Agent Radius and Height in navigation settings to match pawn collision to avoid getting stuck.
Key Takeaway

Nav Areas and agent sizing are essential tools to shape AI movement without changing behavior code.

Practical Notes
If paths look blocky, adjust cell size; if NavMesh generation takes too long, increase cell size. For groups, enable Crowd Manager and tune Separation, Avoidance, and Cohesion to reduce collisions.
Common Mistake
Neglecting Agent Radius/Height, which often causes pawns to get stuck in narrow spaces despite a correct NavMesh.

screens.title: Move To Actor vs Move To Location
screens.narratorSegment: When you instruct an AI to move, you can point to an Actor or to a static Location. Move To Actor tells the pathfinder to follow the actor object; if that actor moves, the node can continuously re-evaluate the path so the AI follows. Move To Location uses a world position stored in the Blackboard and is best for stationary or precomputed destinations. A recommended pattern is to use Move To Actor when chasing a live target and to use a Service that periodically updates the actor’s location into a Blackboard vector only when you need extra control, such as smoothing or offsetting. One misconception is assuming Move To Actor always behaves perfectly for every physics-driven pawn; sometimes updating a vector and using Move To Location gives you more control over offsets and predicted positions. Also be mindful of cancellation and abort modes: if a higher-priority branch becomes active (e. g., Attack), you may want Move To to abort cleanly. Test both approaches in your specific gameplay loop and observe whether path recalculation frequency meets responsiveness without excessive C P U overhead.

keyIdea.text: Use Move To Actor for live targets and Move To Location for static or precomputed destinations; choose the pattern that best balances control and performance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Move To Comparison
Move To Actor

Follow a live target

Directly references a target actor; path is recalculated to follow the actor as it moves.

Pros
  • Automatic re-evaluation for moving actors
  • Simpler setup for chasing behavior
Cons
Less control over offsets and prediction; may need extra logic for physics-driven targets.
Move To Location

Go to a position

Uses a vector location from the Blackboard; ideal for waypoints, patrols, or predicted positions.

Pros
More control for offsets, prediction, and smoothing. Good for patrols and precomputed destinations.
Cons
Requires updating vectors for moving targets; adds a Service or logic to refresh positions.
Check Your Understanding
When would you use Move To Location instead of Move To Actor to implement a flanking maneuver?

screens.title: AI Communication Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: AI characters often need to communicate — alert nearby allies, read a global alert state, or call functions on the player. Prefer loose coupling: Blueprint Interfaces are a robust way to call generic functions like AlertNearbyAllies without casting to a specific class. For example, an I_Alertable interface could define OnAlert; any AI that implements it can respond when another AI spots the player. Event Dispatchers and delegate systems are useful when you want many listeners to respond to an event broadcast, for instance 'EnemySpotted'. Blackboard keys or a GameState variable can serve as global flags indicating alert level; other AI can read that state and adjust behavior. Avoid tight casting between Blueprint classes because it increases fragility and reduces reusability. When designing communication, think about failure modes: ensure receivers are guarded against nulls and provide fallbacks if no listeners exist. Also prefer interfaces for game-wide signals and dispatchers for local, instance-specific subscriptions. Consider how you would design a system where only squad-leader AI signs trigger an alert broadcast to minimize chatter and costly checks across many pawns. AI Communication Patterns means use interfaces and dispatchers for flexible communication; reserve shared blackboards and gamestate variables for global or persistent flags.. In practical terms, interfaces, event dispatchers, and blackboard/global flags. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Patterns

Interfaces & Event Dispatchers

Use interfaces for generic function calls and dispatchers to broadcast events that many objects may subscribe to.

Blueprint Interface Example
Define I_Alertable with OnAlert. Any pawn implementing the interface can be notified without casting.
Event Dispatcher Example
Broadcast EnemySpotted to local listeners; receivers subscribe on BeginPlay and unsubscribe on EndPlay.

GameState or shared Blackboard-like keys can hold global alert status, but use sparingly to avoid accidental coupling between unrelated systems.
Design Tip
Have only designated broadcasters (e.g., squad leaders) send global events to reduce noise and CPU cost from frequent checks across many pawns.

screens.title: Performance & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When many AI characters are active, small design choices multiply into significant C P U cost. First, audit Services: reduce frequency where possible and avoid running heavy line traces every tick across many AI. Use timers or retriggerable delays to space out expensive work. Second, prefer event-driven updates when available; only poll when you must. Third, tune NavMesh cell size and agent settings to balance quality and memory usage. For debugging, use the Behavior Tree Monitor: select the AI Controller at runtime and inspect which nodes are active, which decorators failed, and the current Blackboard values. If a branch never runs, confirm the Blackboard key name, the decorator's query type, and that the Blackboard is actually being updated by the controller. The common failure case described in the chapter is the Chase branch not running despite perception setting TargetActor — this almost always points to a misconfigured Blackboard Based Condition on the Sequence. When profiling, use commands like stat unit to find C P U hotspots and correlate them with Services or heavy Tasks. Always provide clear exit conditions for Tasks to avoid infinite loops that lock up AI controllers.

Reduce expensive updates

Space out Services, avoid per-frame line traces across many AI, and use events when possible.

screens.title: Build BT_EnemyAI — Starter Steps
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through building a simple but robust Behavior Tree for enemy AI. First create BB_EnemyAI with TargetActor (Object) and PatrolLocation (Vector). Then create BT_EnemyAI and in your AI Controller call Run Behavior Tree in BeginPlay. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Starter Activity
Steps

Create Blackboard and Behavior Tree

  1. Create BB_EnemyAI with TargetActor (Object) and PatrolLocation (Vector).
  2. Create BT_EnemyAI and Run Behavior Tree in BP_EnemyAIController BeginPlay.
  3. Hook AIPerception to set/clear TargetActor on the Blackboard.
  4. Build a Selector: Chase Sequence (TargetActor Is Set) and Patrol Sequence (TargetActor Is Not Set).
  5. Add Service to Chase to update target location and a custom BTT_FindRandomPatrolLocation for patrol.
Key Takeaway

Follow the event-driven pattern: perception updates Blackboard, tree decorators gate branches, services refresh dynamic data.

Starter Blueprint Pseudocode
// BP_EnemyAIController OnTargetPerceptionUpdated
If SuccessfullySensed && IsPlayerCharacter:
  Get Blackboard Component (self)
  Set Value As Object(TargetActor, PerceivedActor)
Else:
  Get Blackboard Component (self)
  Clear Value(TargetActor)

// BT_EnemyAI Layout
Root
  Selector
    Sequence (Decorator: TargetActor Is Set)
      Service: BTS_UpdateTargetLocation
      Task: Move To (Blackboard Key: TargetActor)
    Sequence (Decorator: TargetActor Is Not Set)
      Task: BTT_FindRandomPatrolLocation
      Task: Move To (Blackboard Key: PatrolLocation)
      Task: Wait (2.0s)
Validation
Run the Behavior Tree Monitor to confirm keys and branch activity. If Chase doesn't run, inspect the decorator configuration and Blackboard values.

screens.title: Crowd Manager & Group Navigation
screens.narratorSegment: When multiple AI characters navigate the same space, simple pathfinding can lead to unrealistic collisions and bottlenecks. Unreal's Crowd Manager helps by adding parameters like Separation, Avoidance, and Cohesion that produce smoother, more natural group movement. Separation keeps agents apart, Avoidance reduces collisions with near neighbors or obstacles, and Cohesion helps groups stay together when required. Adjust these parameters based on expected group density and desired behavior: high separation suits individualistic enemies, while high cohesion fits squad-based movement. The Crowd Manager works with agent radii and velocities to compute avoidance steering that sits on top of pathfinding. Remember to test with many agents simultaneously; a pattern that looks good with three characters may break with thirty. A common oversight is forgetting to enable any crowd-related settings in project navigation, leaving AI to collide or jitter. For complex interactions, combine Crowd Manager steering with game logic decorators so agents will abort or re-route when group avoidance results in undesirable pathing. Ask yourself how an AI should behave when blocked: should it recalculate, wait, or attempt a different action? Crowd Manager & Group Navigation means use crowd manager to tune separation and avoidance so many agents move naturally without costly per-agent collision handling.. In practical terms, simulating natural group movement and avoiding collisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Crowd Manager
Concept

Separation, Avoidance, Cohesion

Crowd Manager computes steering to reduce collisions and create natural group motion on top of NavMesh pathfinding.

When to use
Whenever many agents move in the same spaces and you need realistic spacing without manual collision handling.
Key Takeaway

Tune crowd parameters and test at scale; what looks fine with a few pawns may need different settings at larger scale.

Practical Tip
Use Separation to prevent overlap, Avoidance for dynamic obstacle steering, and Cohesion to keep platoons together. Combine with decorator logic to avoid deadlocks.
Common Mistake
Not testing with high agent counts and assuming per-agent steering scales linearly; always validate at target population levels.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three core concepts are the foundation for advanced AI in Unreal. First, the Blackboard is your shared memory; keep keys small and explicit so nodes can read state without tight coupling. Second, Behavior Trees compose Composites, Decorators, Tasks, and Services; each node type has a distinct responsibility. Use Selectors for priority, Sequences for ordered steps, Decorators for gating, Tasks for actions, and Services for periodic updates. Third, navigation tuning and communication patterns are essential: use Nav Areas and correct agent settings to shape paths, enable Crowd Manager to smooth group movement, and use interfaces or event dispatchers for loose coupling between AI actors. When debugging, rely on the Behavior Tree Monitor to inspect node status and Blackboard values. For performance, minimize expensive per-frame operations and lower Service frequency where possible. These concepts together let you build adaptive, debuggable, and performant AI systems that respond reliably in dynamic game worlds.

In this lesson you'll explore how Behavior Trees and Blackboards let AI make complex, modular decisions, and how Unreal's navigation systems keep that behavior reliable in dynamic environments. We start by defining the Blackboard as a shared key-value store used to persist things like a current TargetActor or PatrolLocation, then show how a Behavior Tree composes Composites, Decorators, Services, and Tasks to produce reactive AI. You will hear concrete examples: a Selector that prefers Attack, then Chase, then Patrol; a Service that updates the target's location every half second so Move To always has fresh coordinates. We'll also cover NavMesh tuning and Nav Areas so AI can prefer safer routes, and Crowd Manager settings so groups avoid collisions naturally. Finally, you'll practice debugging with the Behavior Tree Monitor and learn common performance traps, such as expensive Services running too often. By the end of this module you will understand how to structure decision logic, connect perception into the Blackboard, and keep AI both responsive and performant. Consider how you would add an Attack branch that respects cooldowns and line of sight.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to design modular AI decision logic with a Blackboard and Behavior Tree, implement advanced navigation strategies using NavMesh and Nav Areas, create specialized Behavior Tree nodes like Tasks, Services, and Decorators, and set up communication between AI agents and the player. First, you'll learn how the Blackboard centralizes data such as TargetActor and PatrolLocation so different tree nodes can access shared state without tight coupling. Second, you'll understand the Behavior Tree node types and how sequences and selectors create ordered and prioritized behavior. Third, you will learn to tune NavMesh and Crowd Manager settings to avoid collisions, prefer safe routes, and handle moving targets. Fourth, you will practice debugging with the Behavior Tree Monitor and learn optimization techniques like reducing Service frequency. Each objective includes a short practice that ties conceptual understanding to a hands-on step. These skills matter because they let you scale AI systems: modular trees with services are easier to extend, NavMesh tuning reduces gameplay bugs, and monitor-driven debugging shortens iteration time. Think about which objective will most change how you approach enemy AI design in your next level.

This second objectives slide focuses on tools and measurable practice. You will integrate the AIPerception component to set and clear Blackboard keys when a player is sensed or lost, so perception directly drives the Behavior Tree. You'll also set up simple services that run at controlled intervals to update moving target locations, avoiding per-frame cost. For navigation, you will learn to assign Nav Areas to geometry and verify Agent Radius and Height in NavMesh settings so your characters don't become trapped. We will also add a small checklist for profiling: check Service frequency, avoid heavy line traces every tick, and use the Behavior Tree Monitor to see which decorators prevent branches from running. Each of these items becomes part of a verified milestone: you can prove correct behavior by observing Blackboard values change and by watching the Monitor show the active branch. These are practical, testable outcomes that shorten iteration time and make AI systems more robust in real levels.

A Blackboard is simply a structured key-value store used by an AI Controller and its Behavior Tree to share state across nodes. Define keys like TargetActor (object), PatrolLocation (vector), or Alerted (bool) and let any Task, Decorator, or Service read or write them. This centralization prevents tight coupling between nodes: a Move To task doesn’t need direct references to the sensing code because it reads the TargetActor key. Concretely, when AIPerception senses the player, the AI Controller sets TargetActor in the Blackboard. The chase Sequence has a Blackboard-based decorator that queries Is Set for TargetActor; when true, the Sequence runs a Move To task using that key. One common misconception is to treat the Blackboard like a global state bag you can overpopulate; instead keep keys explicit and minimal to avoid confusion and costly lookups. Also remember that sharing a Blackboard asset across multiple AI pawns is uncommon; typically each AI has an instance-bound Blackboard Component. When debugging, open the Behavior Tree Monitor and watch the Blackboard tab — you will see keys change in real time which tells you whether the Behavior Tree has data to proceed. How would you structure keys for an AI that can switch between patrol, investigate, and attack?

A Behavior Tree is a hierarchical structure that orchestrates AI decisions. At the root sits the Root node, beneath it Composites like Selector and Sequence control execution order. A Selector tries each child until one succeeds, which is ideal for prioritized choices such as Attack, then Chase, then Patrol. A Sequence executes children in order and fails if any child fails; use it when steps must happen in a strict order, for example Find Cover then Shoot. Decorators are conditional gates placed above nodes — they check Blackboard keys or visibility and allow a branch only if conditions pass. Tasks are leaf nodes that perform actions, like Move To or Play Animation. Services are special nodes that run periodically while their branch is active to update Blackboard keys or perform checks. A misconception is to overuse Services for per-frame checks; prefer half-second intervals and only update what changes. In practice you'll combine these: a Sequence decorated with a 'TargetActor Is Set' decorator contains a Service that refreshes target location and a Move To task that reads that location. Understanding how these parts connect helps you design trees that are both reactive and maintainable. What decision should a Selector prioritize in your game design?

This lesson walks through the concrete process of turning perception into action. The AIPerception component raises an OnTargetPerceptionUpdated event when it senses or loses an actor. In the AI Controller, respond to that event by getting the Blackboard Component and calling Set Value As Object for TargetActor when the player is sensed, and Clear Value when lost. The Behavior Tree’s Chase branch must have a Blackboard-based decorator configured to query Is Set for TargetActor so it activates only when that key exists. To keep the chase accurate when the target moves, add a Service that runs periodically and writes the target's current location into a CurrentTargetLocation or PatrolLocation key. The Move To task should read that key from the Blackboard, or use the Blackboard Key pointing to the actor directly. One typical mistake is forgetting to Run Behavior Tree on BeginPlay in the AI Controller — the tree never runs even if the Blackboard changes. Another debugging step is to open the Behavior Tree Monitor and confirm that the decorator becomes green and the Move To task receives updated positions. As you practice, think about how often your Service needs to run for acceptable responsiveness without wasting C P U.

Tasks are the leaf actions of a Behavior Tree and should represent a single atomic activity, like moving, attacking, or triggering an animation. Services run periodically while a branch is active to update Blackboard keys or perform cheap checks that inform decorators. Decorators evaluate conditions to allow or block branch execution. Choose a custom Blueprint task when you need game-specific work such as selecting a cover point or playing a complex combo animation sequence. Create a Service when you need to refresh data like the target's moving location; for example, a BTS_UpdateTargetLocation service can run every 0.5 seconds to set CurrentTargetLocation on the Blackboard. A common mistake is to pack too much logic into a Task that should instead be a Service plus small tasks — Tasks should finish with success or failure and not run indefinitely. When authoring a Decorator, prefer simple checks: Blackboard Based Condition or Has Line Of Sight To. Use the Behavior Tree Monitor to observe decorator outcomes and service ticks; this will reveal misconfigured keys or improper query types. Consider how you would split behavior between a custom MoveTo wrapper task and services that compute the destination.

Unreal's NavMesh provides the foundation for AI pathfinding and supports dynamic updates when geometry changes. Nav Areas are tags you assign to geometry to influence routing; for instance, a NavArea_Danger can carry a higher traversal cost so AI prefers a longer, safer route. For dynamic scenarios like opened doors or collapsing walls, the NavMesh can be rebuilt or updated at runtime so AI recalculates valid paths. When many agents navigate, use Crowd Manager to tune separation and avoidance so movement looks natural. A common trap is setting cell sizes too small: while this yields finer paths, it increases memory and generation time. Conversely, too large a cell size makes the NavMesh blocky. When AI must follow a moving target, make the Move To node read a Blackboard key that a Service refreshes, ensuring the path is recalculated as the target moves. Consider how you might use a NavArea_Jump to mark spots where AI must use a jump path instead of walking.

When you instruct an AI to move, you can point to an Actor or to a static Location. Also be mindful of cancellation and abort modes: if a higher-priority branch becomes active (e. g., Attack), you may want Move To to abort cleanly.
